To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
patients with schizophrenia have increased levels of plasma antibodies to indigestible gliaden peptides and decreased levels of plasma antibodies of the same type to native gliadins.

the plasma IgG antibodies against the indigestible gliaden-derived peptides are increased in patients with schizophrenia, but the plasma antibodies against native wheat gliadin molecules are not increased.

plasma immunoglobulin A and G antibodies against indigestable peptides derived from wheat gluten were differentially elevated in patients with schizophrenia, compared with control subjects, suggesting that the immune system of patients with schizophrenia is sensitized by gluten-derived peptides that escape digestion.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of a novel biomarker of schizophrenia that is based on the measurement of plasma IgG and IgG antibodies against indigestibly gliadin-derived antigents.
the identification of a subgroup of patients with schizophrenia who may benefit from gluten-free diets.
the development of a novel approach for detection of antibodies against indigestable gliadin-derived antigents in plasma of patients with schizophrenia.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
patients with schizophrenia have an altered immune response to gliadin-derived peptide fragments.
the differential antibody response to indigestible gliadins is not a common phenomenon in schizophrenia, although the possibility of its occurrence in a subgroup of patients cannot be ruled out.
the increased levels of IgG against AAQ6C in the plasma of patients with schizophrenia could be a potential biomarker for the identification of a subgroup of patients with schizophrenia.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the increased plasma IgG antibodies against indigestibly gliadin-derived peptides may be involved in the pathogenesis of schizophrenia, and that the decreased plasma IgA antibodies may reflect a defect in the mucosal immunity in patients with the disease.
schizophrenia is an immunological disorder, in which the immune system is dysregulated and the body is unable to mount a proper immune response to gluten.
the differential antibody responses to gliadins and gliadin-derived antigents may provide new clues to understanding the pathophysiology of schizophrenia.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the differential responses of antibodies against indigestibly gliadin-derived antigents in patients with schizophrenia suggest a potential role of these antibodies in the pathophysiology of this illness.

the immune system in patients with schizophrenia responds differently to indigestible gliadins than to native gliadins, suggesting that gliadin-derived peptides, not native gliadins or gliadin-derived amino acid fragments, may be responsible for the immunological abnormalities in patients with schizophrenia.
the differential antibody responses against indigestible gluten peptides may provide a new perspective on the role of gluten in the pathogenesis of schizophrenia.
